Visitors can also see the Gaval Dash, a stone that makes a sound like a tambourine when struck, and mud volcanoes nearby that bubble with cold mud.

UNESCO inscribed the Gobustan Rock Art Cultural Landscape as a World Heritage Site in 2007. A modern museum on the site explains the finds and the history of the region.

articles.title: Maiden Tower
articles.description: Baku's mysterious medieval symbol.
articles.content:
The Maiden Tower, or Giz Galasi, is a stone tower in the Old City of Baku and one of the best-known symbols of Azerbaijan. It is about 30 metres tall and has eight floors, with walls up to five metres thick at the base.

It was built in the 12th century, although its exact purpose is unclear: scholars have suggested that it served as a watchtower, a Zoroastrian temple or an observatory. The name has led to many legends, including the story of a princess who leapt from its top to escape an unwanted marriage.

The tower is part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site of the Old City, and its image appears on money and in art. Visitors can climb inside for panoramic views of Baku and the Caspian.

articles.title: Flame Towers
articles.description: Baku's three glowing skyscrapers.
articles.content:
The Flame Towers are three skyscrapers in Baku, completed in 2012, whose curved shapes recall tongues of fire. They refer to Azerbaijan's title of Land of Fire, and are visible from many parts of the city.

The tallest tower is over 180 metres. The complex contains offices, apartments and a hotel, and the surfaces are covered with LED screens that display flames, the Azerbaijani flag and other images at night. The towers stand on a hill above the seaside boulevard.

They became a symbol of modern Baku and a popular subject for photographers. Together with the Old City and the Heydar Aliyev Center, they show the contrast between old and new in the city's skyline.

articles.title: Heydar Aliyev Center
articles.description: A flowing building designed by Zaha Hadid.
articles.content:
The Heydar Aliyev Center is a cultural complex in Baku, designed by the Iraqi-British architect Zaha Hadid and completed in 2012. Its curved white form flows out of the ground with almost no straight lines or sharp corners.

The building includes a museum, exhibition halls and an auditorium, and covers about 57,000 square metres. It is built from a concrete structure and a steel framework covered with panels that create its smooth surface. Hadid wanted the building to express optimism and a break from rigid Soviet-era architecture.

In 2014 the Center won the Design Museum's Design of the Year award, and it has become one of the most photographed buildings in the world.

articles.title: Palace of the Shirvanshahs
articles.description: The royal palace complex in Baku's Old City.
articles.content:
The Palace of the Shirvanshahs is a medieval palace complex in the Old City of Baku, built mostly in the 15th century for the Shirvanshahs, the rulers of the state of Shirvan. The complex includes the main palace, the Divankhana, a mosque, a mausoleum and a bath.

The buildings are made of local limestone and show the Shirvan-Absheron school of architecture, with restrained decoration and carved inscriptions. The Divankhana is an octagonal pavilion with a domed portal, thought to have been used for receptions and judicial meetings.

The palace is part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site of the Walled City of Baku. Restored in the 20th century, it is now a museum that presents the history of the Shirvanshahs.

articles.title: Sheki Khan's Palace
articles.description: The summer palace with stained-glass windows.
articles.content:
The Palace of the Sheki Khans is a palace built in 1797 as the summer residence of the rulers of the Sheki Khanate. It is a two-storey building in the centre of Sheki, next to a fortress and a large plane tree.

Its windows are made of shebeke, a lattice of small pieces of coloured glass fitted into wooden frames without glue or nails. The walls and ceilings are decorated with colourful murals of flowers, hunting scenes and landscapes, and the palace has six rooms.

The palace is the main attraction of Sheki, a city known for its Silk Road history. UNESCO inscribed the Historic Centre of Sheki with the Khan's Palace as a World Heritage Site in 2019.

articles.title: Baku
articles.description: The capital on the shore of the Caspian Sea.
articles.content:
Baku is the capital and largest city of Azerbaijan, a port on the western shore of the Caspian Sea, on the Absheron Peninsula. More than two million people live in the city, which is one of the lowest-lying capitals in the world.

The city is known for its historic Old City, its winds and its oil. In the second half of the 19th century the oil boom brought great wealth, and families such as the Nobels, Rothschilds and local oil barons built grand buildings. The seaside boulevard, the Flame Towers and the Heydar Aliyev Center reflect the modern city.

Baku has hosted major events, including the Eurovision Song Contest in 2012, the first European Games in 2015 and the Azerbaijan Grand Prix of Formula 1 since 2016. It is also the country's cultural centre, with theatres, museums and universities.

articles.title: Ganja
articles.description: Azerbaijan's second city, the home of Nizami.
articles.content:
Ganja is the second-largest city of Azerbaijan, in the west of the country at the foot of the Lesser Caucasus. It is more than a thousand years old and was a major cultural and trading centre along the Silk Road.

It is the birthplace of the poet Nizami Ganjavi, whose mausoleum stands in the city. Historic sites include the Javad Khan Gate, the Juma Mosque and the Shah Abbas Mosque, and the tourism area around Lake Goygol is nearby. The city is also known for its cuisine and sweets.

In 1918 the government of the Azerbaijan Democratic Republic first met in Ganja. Today it is a centre of industry, education and culture, and it has a lively park and cafe scene.

articles.title: Sheki
articles.description: The Silk Road city in the Caucasus foothills.
articles.content:
Sheki is a historic city in northern Azerbaijan, set in the foothills of the Greater Caucasus mountains. It was an important stop on the Silk Road and became a centre for silk production, which is still traded today.

The city is known for the Palace of the Sheki Khans, built in 1797, and the 18th-century Sheki Caravanserai, once used by traveling merchants and now a hotel. Its old streets are lined with houses that have red-tiled roofs and shebeke windows. The Kish Albanian church nearby is one of the oldest Christian sites in the region.

Sheki is famous for its sweets, including Sheki halva, a layered rice-flour pastry, and its piti stew. UNESCO inscribed the Historic Centre of Sheki as a World Heritage Site in 2019.

articles.title: Karabakh Horse
articles.description: The golden-coated national horse of Azerbaijan.
articles.content:
The Karabakh horse is a breed of riding horse developed in the Karabakh region of Azerbaijan, and it is regarded as the country's national horse. It is known for its endurance, speed and gentle temperament, and for the golden or chestnut coat with a metallic shine.

For centuries the breed was used by cavalry and nomads in the mountains, and Karabakh horses were also sent as gifts to rulers. The breed is smaller than many Western breeds, but strong and adapted to hills and hot weather, and it was used to improve other breeds.

The horse plays a key role in chovgan, a traditional horse-riding game similar to polo, which UNESCO inscribed on its list of intangible cultural heritage in 2013. Breeders work to protect this rare breed.

articles.title: Origami
articles.description: The Japanese art of paper folding, from cranes to modern engineering.
articles.content:
Origami is the traditional Japanese art of folding paper into decorative or representational shapes, without cutting or gluing. The word combines the Japanese words for folding, oru, and paper, kami. Paper folding developed after papermaking reached Japan from China around the 6th century, and it was originally used mainly for ceremonial purposes.

The crane is the best-known origami figure and a symbol of peace and long life. In 1955 a Japanese girl named Sadako Sasaki, who became ill after the atomic bombing of Hiroshima, folded paper cranes in the hope of recovering, inspired by a legend that folding a thousand cranes grants a wish; her story made the crane a worldwide symbol of peace, and children still send folded cranes to a memorial in Hiroshima.

Modern origami has grown far beyond traditional shapes. Mathematicians and engineers now study the geometry of folding to design compact solar panels that unfold in space, foldable medical stents and even airbags, and origami principles are taught in schools worldwide as a simple way to explore geometry and patience with nothing more than a square of paper.
